svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Microsoft Entra Seamless SSO works and where its risk sits. Enabling the feature creates one AZUREADSSOACC computer account per Active Directory forest, with a number of Kerberos service principal names, and the computer account's Kerberos decryption key is shared with Microsoft Entra ID, each forest having its own unique key. In the browser flow, Microsoft Entra ID challenges the browser with a 401 Unauthorized response using JavaScript, the browser requests a Kerberos ticket from Active Directory for the AZUREADSSOACC account, Active Directory returns a ticket encrypted with that account's secret, the browser forwards it, and Microsoft Entra ID decrypts it with the previously shared key to learn the identity of the signed-in user, then either issues a token or asks for multifactor authentication. The feature is opportunistic, so if it fails the user simply types a password. The native client flow instead retrieves a WS-Trust MEX endpoint used exclusively by this feature, obtains a Kerberos challenge, and exchanges a SAML token at the OAuth2 token endpoint for an access token, refresh token and ID token. The risk panel quotes that the Kerberos decryption key, if leaked, can be used to generate Kerberos tickets for any synchronized user, with the mitigation being a rollover at least every 30 days using the Update-AzureADSSOForest cmdlet, which must not be run more than once per forest or the feature stops working until users' Kerberos tickets expire. Client-side conditions include adding the autologon URL to the intranet zone with a value of 1, enabling Allow updates to status bar via script, Microsoft 365 clients at version 16.0.8730.xxxx or later, a device joined to Windows Server AD but not necessarily Microsoft Entra joined, and a direct connection to a domain controller. A final panel notes the July 2026 Windows Server update changes the default Kerberos encryption type in AD DS from RC4 to AES-256, and that the key must be rolled over before switching encryption type.
svg.title: One computer account represents Microsoft Entra ID inside your forest, and its key is the whole boundary
svg.text: A free checkbox creates one computer account that represents Microsoft Entra ID inside your directory.
“The computer account’s Kerberos decryption key is shared securely with Microsoft Entra ID.” That key is the security boundary.
The browser flow: Entra learns who you are from a ticket your own domain controller issued
Entra challenges the browser in the background with a 401 Unauthorized, asking for a Kerberos ticket
The browser asks Active Directory for a ticket for AZUREADSSOACC — the account that represents Entra
AD returns a ticket “encrypted with the computer account’s secret”; the browser forwards it
Entra decrypts it with the shared key and reads the identity of the user signed into the device
Entra then “either returns a token… or asks the user to perform additional proofs, such as MFA”
So the password prompt disappears and the Conditional Access evaluation does not. And the whole thing is opportunistic:
“if it fails, the sign-in experience falls back to its regular behavior” — no error, no report, just a password prompt.
The risk, in Microsoft’s own words
“The Kerberos decryption key on a computer account, if
leaked, can be used to generate Kerberos tickets for any
synchronized user.”
Mitigation: roll it over at least every 30 days, with
Update-AzureADSSOForest, on the Connect server.
But never twice per forest: a second run stops sign-in
“until the time your users’ Kerberos tickets expire”.
The admin running it must not be in Protected Users, or
the operation fails — hardening breaking the hygiene task.
What has to be true on the client
“Browsers don’t send Kerberos tickets to a cloud endpoint…
unless you explicitly add the URL to the intranet zone.”
Group Policy: the autologon URL at zone value 1, plus
“Allow updates to status bar via script”. Value 4 excludes.
Domain-joined — but “doesn’t need to be Microsoft Entra
joined”. Needs a direct connection to a domain controller,
so it does not work from a coffee shop.
Office apps need 16.0.8730.xxxx or later, and take a
different path: WS-Trust MEX, then a SAML token.
A dated change that has already landed
“Starting with the July 2026 Windows Server update, the default Kerberos encryption type in AD DS will change from RC4
to AES-256. Organizations that continue to use RC4 may experience authentication or Seamless SSO issues.”
Order matters: roll the key FIRST, then change the encryption type. Doing it the intuitive way round can break SSO.
Supported types: AES256_HMAC_SHA1, AES128_HMAC_SHA1, RC4_HMAC_MD5 — recorded in msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes.
Where the silence is worst: the feature’s own status
Disabled with PowerShell
“won’t change the state in Microsoft Entra Connect” — the wizard still says Enabled
Clean-up after disabling
manual: delete the AZUREADSSO computer account from each forest yourself
A broken rollout
looks exactly like life before the feature: users just type passwords
Credential-theft hardening in place
the account must be kept out of the Quarantine container, by exception
What it is not, and what replaces it
Works with password hash sync and pass-through authentication; “this feature can’t be used with Active Directory Federation
Services.” It is free, and needs no paid edition of Microsoft Entra ID. Multiple forests are supported, with or without trusts.
Microsoft Entra join does SSO with primary refresh tokens rather than Kerberos, and “takes precedence over Seamless SSO”
where both are on. So the 30-day obligation belongs to a transitional feature — worth knowing what would let you drop it.
Configuration screens report intent. Go and look at the object.
Sources: Seamless SSO — How it works, Quickstart: Microsoft Entra seamless single sign-on, and Seamless SSO FAQ, on Microsoft Learn.
